title: Kauders v. Uber Technologies, Inc.
lead: Riders challenging guide-dog refusals were sent to arbitration based on Uber’s registration screens. Although the trial judge later used the wrong procedure to undo that order, the state high court reached the preserved formation question and held that the interface provided neither reasonable notice nor assent.

actors.name: Christopher and Hannah Kauders
actors.role: Riders disputing formation of Uber’s online agreement

actors.name: Justice Kafker
actors.role: Author of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court opinion

proceedings: The Superior Court compelled arbitration, then reconsidered after an award for Uber instead of confirming it. The Supreme Judicial Court found that procedure erroneous but resolved the preserved formation issue, held the dispute nonarbitrable, and remanded.
limits: The court decided this registration process and record, not discrimination liability, universal online-contract validity, or a disability-specific accessibility standard. It did not adjudicate every substantive term’s enforceability.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The riders registered through practical account-setup screens
sections.cue: Describe the interface before the legal dispute.
paragraphs: Christopher Kauders, who was blind and used a guide dog, registered for Uber on June 27, 2014. Hannah Kauders registered around October 2015. Christopher’s mobile process began with a dark CREATE AN ACCOUNT screen requesting email, phone, and password for ride confirmations and receipts. CREATE A PROFILE then requested a name and optional photo to help drivers identify him. NEXT buttons advanced both screens without directing attention to contracts.

The third screen, LINK PAYMENT, emphasized a white credit-card field, card scanning and promo-code options, and a prominent PayPal button. At the bottom, a sentence said account creation meant agreement to Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy. The introductory explanation was less prominent than the link. Opening it led to another screen and another click to reach terms. A credit-card keypad could move the notice toward the middle, but the final button read DONE rather than I agree and did not expressly identify acceptance.

sections.title: Broad terms became important after alleged ride refusals
sections.cue: Introduce the claims and arbitration outcome.
paragraphs: The terms extended beyond individual rides: amendment without notice, broad liability and warranty disclaimers, indemnification, extensive data use or disclosure, conduct obligations, and near the end an arbitration clause tied to limited damages. Uber would even invoke indemnification to seek the cost of the Kauderses’ court suit. These provisions explained the significance of meaningful notice, without requiring decision of every provision’s validity.

The couple sued Uber Technologies and wholly owned Rasier in July 2016, alleging three drivers refused Christopher rides because of disability and his guide dog. Uber moved to compel in June 2017, partly relying on the federal district court’s Cullinane decision about registration. The Kauderses disputed formation and other defenses. The judge compelled without formation analysis and retained award jurisdiction.

On June 4, 2018, the arbitrator found discriminatory acts by drivers but ruled for Uber because they were independent contractors rather than employees. Three weeks later the First Circuit reversed Cullinane, finding inadequate notice in the same registration process. The Kauderses did not immediately notify the judge or seek award vacatur.

sections.title: Reconsideration followed confirmation efforts too late
sections.cue: Explain the statutory procedure and preserved objection.
paragraphs: Uber moved to confirm in September. At an October hearing the Kauderses invoked Cullinane, and at the judge’s invitation sought reconsideration in November. On January 2, 2019, more than six months after the award, he vacated his original order and denied arbitration and confirmation for lack of contract. Uber appealed, and the Supreme Judicial Court transferred the case.

Justice Kafker explained that Massachusetts law permitted immediate appeal from denial of arbitration but not compulsion. A resisting party could preserve its objection and appeal after confirmation, allowing uninterrupted arbitration without losing review of consent. Thirty-day award challenges mainly concerned arbitration or award defects. Section 12(a)(5) allowed no-agreement vacatur only if that issue had not already been adversely decided in compulsion proceedings and participation was not without objection. Here formation had been decided adversely, so it could not be relitigated that way; compelled participation did not waive the preserved objection.

The judge should therefore have confirmed. Judges generally could correct interlocutory errors without changed law or facts, contrary to Uber’s broader assertion, but completed arbitration and expiration of challenge time constrained that power. Reconsideration was an abuse of discretion. A remand merely for confirmation and inevitable appeal, however, would return the same fully briefed issue. The high court decided formation immediately for judicial economy.

sections.title: Arbitration policy could not substitute for consent
paragraphs: Ordinary state contract law controlled whether any agreement existed. Uber bore the burden of showing reasonable notice of terms and a reasonable manifestation of assent. The court imposed no separate conspicuousness requirement.

Actual notice sufficed; otherwise all circumstances mattered, including transaction type and scale, contractual appearance, presentation and placement, access steps, and clarity about what action meant acceptance. An affirmative I agree button was strong, readily implemented evidence, but not indispensable if another action clearly communicated assent.

sections.title: Neither notice nor the meaning of DONE was adequate
sections.cue: Apply each requirement to these screens.
paragraphs: Registration appeared to arrange future small rides, not announce expansive data, liability, indemnity, and arbitration obligations. The design directed attention to payment fields and prominent alternatives. Other large features weakened the link’s salience. Uber’s claim that the notice sat centrally depended on activating a particular credit-card keypad; the limited record did not establish meaningful presentation on other paths, rather than affirmatively proving every path hid it.

DONE naturally completed payment entry. No adjacent clear instruction made its click contractual acceptance. The sentence highlighted the terms label while downplaying the language establishing legal significance, and registration could finish without opening or acknowledging terms. Other Uber driver interfaces required affirmative acceptance and a second confirmation, demonstrating feasibility of clearer assent, not importing driver contracts into rider transactions. Both requirements failed.

sections.title: The preserved formation challenge succeeded
sections.cue: State the final outcome without deciding discrimination liability.
paragraphs: The court held there was no enforceable agreement with the Kauderses and the dispute was not arbitrable, then remanded for consistent proceedings. It awarded no discrimination damages and did not determine Uber’s ultimate responsibility for its drivers. Its objective notice analysis was not a blindness-specific accessibility ruling.
Kafker wrote without a separate opinion. Lenk, Gaziano, Lowy, Budd, Cypher, and Kafker were listed as participating; Lenk had deliberated before retirement.
